title: Microsoft SQL Server Automation: Agent vs Other Tools
summary: Microsoft SQL Server automation executes scheduled tasks like backups and maintenance.
body_markdown:
## Stage 3: Send SQL Server results to other apps with Activepieces


Use[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/docs/install/reference/limits) when a query result has to land somewhere SQL Server can't reach on its own, such as a Slack channel or an inbox. The flow is a schedule trigger, a Microsoft SQL Server query action, then a message step.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


Index rebuilds, backups and integrity checks stay in Agent, because nothing in them leaves the database.


If the app you need to reach has no connector, Activepieces lets you generate one with AI and add it privately to your own instance, so no vendor release stands in the way.


The 750 integrations in the catalogue are counted from the` packages/pieces/community` directory of the open source monorepo on GitHub (25,549 stars), and roughly 60% of them were contributed by the community, meaning most of the integrations available here are built by volunteer developers.


The core is MIT-licensed, while the enterprise directories in` packages/ee/` carry a separate commercial licence.


### Create a read-only SQL login for the workflow


Give the workflow its own login rather than borrowing a DBA account. Create the login, map it to a user in the one database the query reads, and add that user to the` db_datareader` role.


If the workflow is ever misconfigured, the worst it can do is read what you already allowed.


You will trip on two prerequisites. The instance must accept SQL authentication (mixed mode), since a Windows-only instance rejects a username and password.


And Activepieces must have a network path to the instance, which means TCP/IP enabled and a firewall rule for the host where Activepieces runs.


A cloud-hosted workflow can't see a server that only answers inside your LAN, though the MIT-licensed core can be self-hosted on a machine inside it.


### Add the schedule trigger and the SQL query action


Start with the Schedule trigger and set the interval. Then add the Microsoft SQL Server integration and choose its query action.


The connection asks for the server address, database, and the login and password you just created.


Match those fields against what your Activepieces version shows, since integrations change between releases; the integrations' source lives in the` packages/pieces/community` directory of the monorepo, where you can read it.


Nothing in the builder tells you yet that the connection works. It shows a Schedule trigger labeled "Every Hour" selected, a settings panel with a "Run on weekends" toggle, and a Generate Sample Data result that passed. That passing test proves the trigger fires.


Picking the next step opens an integration selector, and it's worth ignoring the spreadsheet integrations that crowd the first results. You want the SQL Server integration, then a Slack or email integration.


Paste in a query that returns a small, already-aggregated result, such as failed job names from the last day. Run the step's test and check the sample output: the column names there are what you'll reference downstream.


### Post the result to Slack or email


Add the Slack integration's send-message action, pick the channel, and build the text from the query step's output fields. Map the specific columns you need rather than dumping the whole row set. An unfiltered result pasted into a channel gets muted within a week.


For email, the same mapping applies to the subject and body. Use whichever your team actually reads.


Finish by running the full flow once by hand. One query result, posted to one channel, is the whole point. If that works, publish the flow and let the schedule take over.
